item.title: After PHP Gate: A Blueprint for the Static Web
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Last Wednesday, the PHP project shipped four releases in one afternoon. PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fixed two flaws that allow unauthenticated remote code execution, both rated critical at CVSS 9.2:

  • CVE-2026-109618, “RCE via OOM corruption” (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w)
  • CVE-2026-109619, “RCE via stale global state” (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp)

The advisory is short and does not leave much room for interpretation: the flaws affect “all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed,” and “there are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice.” Details had leaked a day before the embargo lifted, honeypots started seeing attempts soon after, and for the rest of the week hosting providers, agencies and WordPress admins were patching, checking, and patching again. Most people call the flaws PHP2Shell. I have been calling the week PHP Gate.

The scale is what makes it a gate rather than a bug. PHP runs 69.2% of the websites whose server-side language W3Techs can identify, and WordPress alone runs 39.6% of all websites. Laravel, MediaWiki (so, Wikipedia), Drupal, Magento: the productive web is still, to a large degree, a PHP interpreter that executes for every single request. When the interpreter has a hole, every one of those requests is a way in.

I do not want to pile on PHP. The PHP team handled this well, and the language has carried more of the web than any other. What worries me is a habit that goes far beyond PHP: running code on a server, at request time, to produce a page that is almost always the same page it produced a second ago. Most of the sites caught up in PHP Gate could have been a folder of files, with no runtime for anyone to attack.

This post is the blueprint I use instead. I looked at every web project I have built over the last few years, about forty sites, documentation sites and web apps across several GitHub organisations, and wrote down what they all do. The practices turned out to be the same every time. There are two template repositories at the end you can clone. The blueprint is not the answer to everything, either, so there is also a section on when a project needs a real backend, and what I build those with.

If “static” and “dynamic” are fuzzy terms for you, read the next section first; it explains them without assuming anything. If you build websites for a living, skip ahead to the shape of it.

Static and dynamic, in plain words

Every time you open a web page, your browser asks a computer somewhere (a server) for it, and the server sends back a file of HTML that the browser draws. The difference between a static and a dynamic website is when that file is made.

A dynamic website makes the page at the moment you ask for it. A program on the server (WordPress, written in PHP, is the most common one) reads a template, asks a database for the article, fills the article into the template, and sends you the result. Then it does the same thing again for the next visitor, and the next, usually producing exactly the same page. It is a kitchen that cooks every plate to order, even when everybody orders the same dish.

dynamic:  you ──► server ──► PHP runs ──► database ──► page is assembled ──► you
                  (for every visitor, every time)

A static website makes every page once, ahead of time, whenever the content changes. A program called a static site generator (this site uses one called Zola) reads all the articles and templates and writes out a folder of finished HTML files. That folder is copied to a CDN, a network of servers around the world that does nothing but hand out files quickly from somewhere close to you. When you ask for a page, nothing is cooked. The finished file is simply handed over.

static:   writer ──► build, once per change ──► folder of files ──► CDN
          you ──► CDN ──► the finished file ──► you
                  (nothing runs when you visit)

Static does not mean boring or frozen. A static page can still be interactive, because the interactivity runs in your browser: menus, search, maps, even a chess engine. What a static site does not have is a program on a server that runs because you visited, which is the part PHP Gate attacked.

A few more words this post uses, so they do not get in the way later:

  • Edge means the CDN’s servers close to the reader. An edge function (Cloudflare calls them Workers) is a small program that runs there, for the rare jobs a file cannot do, like accepting a form.
  • Build is the step that turns content and templates into the finished files. It runs when a change is merged, not when someone visits.
  • Backend is a program on a server that the website talks to: it stores data, checks passwords, takes payments. A static site has no backend of its own; an app may still need one.
  • WebAssembly lets code written in languages like Rust run inside the browser, close to the speed of a native program.
  • Agents are AI assistants that read websites on someone’s behalf. They read static pages especially well.

The idea in one paragraph

Render at commit time, serve files from the edge, and run code only where it cannot be avoided. A page is built once, when a change is merged, and from then on it is a file on a CDN. Logic that must react to a visitor moves to one of two places: the visitor’s own browser (JavaScript, or Rust compiled to WebAssembly when the work is heavy), or a small edge function that does exactly one job, the pattern I described in Edge Systems Are the New Backend. There is no application server, no database behind the pages, and no runtime to patch at two in the morning, because there is nothing running between the request and the file.

Why bother

Security. A static page cannot be exploited the way PHP Gate was exploited, because a request for it never executes anything. The attack surface shrinks to the CDN (which is someone else’s full-time job), the build (which runs in a throwaway container on merge, not on request), and whatever edge functions you choose to add. On most of my sites that last list has zero or one entries. You still have a supply chain to care about, which is why pinning and review matter so much later in this post, but you no longer have an interpreter facing the internet.

Operations. A static site has no server of its own to patch, scale or restart. During PHP Gate my static sites needed nothing from me. A traffic spike is the CDN’s problem, and the CDN was built for it. Rollback is a redeploy of the previous commit, a single click in the Pages dashboard.

Speed and cost. Files from an edge cache are as fast as the web gets, and serving them costs next to nothing: Cloudflare Pages hosts a static site on its free plan with up to 20,000 files.

Longevity. A folder of HTML ages better than almost any other software. Sites I built years ago still render exactly as they did, with no framework upgrade, no runtime end of life, no database migration. PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on 31 December; a static site has no such date.

Machines. More of my readers are now agents, and static pages are simple for them to fetch and parse. If you also publish each page as Markdown and describe it with structured data, they read it correctly.

There are real counterarguments:

  • Dynamic features. Comments, forms, search, accounts, payments. Most of them have a static-friendly form: search runs in the browser over a prebuilt index, forms post to an edge function, comments become pull requests or issues. Some things genuinely need a server, and then you should run one; the next section is about those. The point is to run it for those things only, not for every page view.
  • Editors who do not use Git. This is the real reason WordPress wins in many organisations, and the blueprint does not fully solve it. GitHub’s web editor and issue forms get non-technical contributors surprisingly far, and an agent can turn a Word document into a pull request. For a newsroom with forty editors, I would think harder.
  • Vendor dependence. I lean on Cloudflare. Everything I deploy is still just files in Git, so moving hosts is an afternoon. This site is served by GitHub Pages behind Cloudflare, and every push goes to Codeberg as well as GitHub.
  • Build times. A large site takes minutes to build, not milliseconds to render. My largest project takes about a minute for ten languages; Cloudflare’s build limit is twenty minutes. Precomputing data in separate build steps keeps it there.

When you do need a backend

Some projects are not websites with a few interactive parts. They are services, and pretending otherwise produces a pile of edge functions that slowly turns into a backend nobody designed. These are the signs I look for:

  • People have accounts and their own data. Logins, profiles, private documents, per-user settings that must follow them across devices.
  • Many people write, not just read. A marketplace, a forum, a booking system, an internal tool where every user changes shared state.
  • Things happen in real time between users. Chat, collaborative editing, live dashboards, presence.
  • The work is heavy, long, or secret. Jobs that run for minutes, data that cannot be shipped to the browser, integrations that need credentials, money moving between parties.
  • The data does not fit in a build. Millions of records that change by the minute cannot be rendered into files on every merge.

When two or more of these are true, I build a backend, and I pick it by the shape of the problem:

The projectWhat I reach forWhy
An API: endpoints, data, integrationsGoOne static binary, a fast start, modest memory, an excellent standard library for HTTP, and concurrency that is easy to reason about.
A rich app frontend that renders per userNext.js, or a framework like itServer rendering where a page depends on who is looking, static export where it does not, and the largest ecosystem of components and people.
A service that is distributed by nature: real time, many connections, many nodesElixir and PhoenixThe BEAM was built for exactly this: lightweight processes, supervision that restarts what fails, clustering, PubSub and LiveView without bolting on extra infrastructure.
The same, with a type system that catches mistakes at compile timeRefraktMy own framework, in Gleam on the BEAM: productive like Phoenix, explicit like Gleam, with generators for the routine parts. Still young; I use it where I can follow its changes.

Two of my own services show the Phoenix row in practice: Cyanea runs Phoenix on SQLite, and Archipelag.io runs Phoenix with Postgres and NATS. Both run on one bare-metal server, which I wrote about in How AI Makes Bare Metal Viable Again.

Even with a backend, most of the blueprint still applies. A service with a real backend has parts that are just content: the landing page, the documentation, the changelog, the legal pages, the blog. Those stay static, on the blueprint, and the backend is a separate deployment with a small, well-defined API. The rest of the lessons carry over unchanged: agent context first, the data types declared before the code, pinned versions, and as little running at request time as the problem allows. And keep the PHP Gate lesson close: a backend is a runtime facing the internet, so it needs an owner, an update routine, and the discipline to keep it no bigger than it has to be.

The shape of it

Every project of mine, from a one-page product site to a ten-language knowledge base, has the same shape:

  GitHub organisation (one per product)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ .github   .claude  theme  content   site    app     worker │
  │ profile   context  Zola   Markdown  config  Svelte  edge   │
  │ policies  rules    Tera   + data    build   + Rust  logic  │
  └───────────────────┬──────┬─────────┬───────┬───────┬───────┘
                      └──────┴─────────┤       │       │
                                       │       │       │    theme and content: submodules,
                                       ▼       ▼       ▼           pinned and reviewed
                                 ┌───────────────────┐┌─────────┐
                                 │ Cloudflare Pages  ││ Workers │
                                 │ files at the edge ││ one job │
                                 └─────────┬─────────┘└────┬────┘
                                           ▼               ▼
                    readers and agents: HTML, Markdown, JSON-LD, llms.txt

Content, presentation and distribution live apart. The content repository holds Markdown and data and nothing else. The theme repository holds templates and styles. The site repository pins both as git submodules, adds configuration, and is the thing Cloudflare builds. Apps get their own repository, and edge functions either live next to the site or in their own. Each repository has one job, so each one is small enough to reason about, and an agent working in it does not have to load the world.

The practices

I found eleven practices that every mature project of mine follows, and that the younger ones are converging on. They are listed roughly in the order I set them up.

1. Start with the agent context, before the first line of code

The first file in every repository is AGENTS.md, and in a Claude Code project CLAUDE.md simply imports it (@AGENTS.md) and adds the Claude-specific parts. I write it before any code, as the contract the repository works under: the stack, where each kind of content is registered, what is generated and must never be edited, how to verify a change, and the rules that always hold. On this site it starts like this:

The short version: **content is registered once, in a source file; everything else is generated.**
Never edit a generated file by hand. If a new piece of content does not show up somewhere it should,
the fix is in the source file or in the generator, not in the output.

Then come the rules, in .claude/rules/, one file per kind of task (content, templates, Rust), each scoped to the paths it applies to. Then skills, in .claude/skills/, for the workflows that repeat: add a page end to end, publish an article, translate. My most mature project goes further: an organisation-level context repository that every repository’s AGENTS.md points to, subagents with restricted tools (the reviewer is read-only and forms its verdict before it sees the editor’s report), and an explicit list of changes that require a human.

Writing it first costs an hour. In return, every later session, mine or an agent’s, starts from the same understanding, and the decisions the rest of this list depends on are made before they are needed.

2. Declare the ontology before you write the content

Every site knows a small number of kinds of thing: articles, notes, projects, talks, books, topics. I declare them up front, each with its register (where instances live), its required fields, its allowed values, and the schema.org type it becomes for machines. In the blueprint this is data/kinds.toml:

[kinds.article]
register = "content/articles/"
required = ["title", "date", "description", "taxonomies.topics"]
optional = ["updated", "draft", "extra.author", "extra.image"]
jsonld = "BlogPosting"

[kinds.project]
register = "data/projects.toml"
required = ["slug", "title", "description", "status", "url", "topics"]
jsonld = "SoftwareApplication"
enum.status = ["live", "beta", "early", "archived"]

A validator enforces it on every pull request, using only the Python standard library so it runs anywhere. Unknown fields fail, so a typo in descripton cannot silently drop a page’s description. Topics come from one vocabulary, with broader links that turn the vocabulary into a small graph. On this site the same declarations drive the map (the story of how it came about is in This Site Is Becoming a Map), the search index, the JSON-LD and the ontology page that explains all of it to readers.

The payoff is that nothing is improvised later. When I add a reading log, a talk, or a new kind of project, the question is “what kind is it, and where is it registered,” not “where should I put this file.”

3. One GitHub organisation per product, one job per repository

A personal account mixes everything. An organisation gives a product its own members, its own secrets, its own profile, and room for the repositories it will grow into. I start with the same set:

RepositoryJob
.githubOrganisation profile, shared issue forms, SECURITY.md, contributing guide
.claudeOrganisation-wide agent context: rules, skills, decisions, plans
themeThe Zola theme, versioned on its own
contentMarkdown and data, validated in CI
siteConfiguration and build, pins theme and content as submodules
app, workerOnly when the product needs them

Two rules keep this healthy. Submodule URLs are HTTPS, so the Cloudflare build can clone them without SSH keys. And the theme is never copied into a site: I found one organisation where five copies of a theme had drifted from the original in fourteen to eighteen template files each. A submodule pin makes drift a visible commit instead of an invisible fork.

4. GitHub is the content store and the moderation layer

There is no admin panel, because Git already is one. Every change is a pull request with a diff, a review and a history. CODEOWNERS says who must approve changes to content, headers and edge code. An issue form collects corrections with a required URL and a dropdown for what is wrong. Contributors submit a pull request from a fork, and the validator runs before a human looks.

Reader input lands in the same place. The blueprint’s only edge function takes the feedback form from every page and files it as a GitHub issue in the content repository, with mentions defused so nobody can ping your team through your own site. Feedback, corrections and contributions all end up in one queue, moderated by the same people with the same tools, and nothing a stranger types ever reaches a page without a review.

Put together, every change follows the same path, whoever starts it:

  reader      ──► feedback form ──► Worker ──► GitHub issue ──► triaged ──┐
  editor      ──► branch ─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  contributor ──► fork ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
                                                                          │
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ▼
  pull request to the content repository
  │   CI validates the ontology, builds the site, runs the tests
  ▼
  review and approval by CODEOWNERS, then merge to main
  │   a workflow in the content repository calls the Pages deploy hook
  ▼
  Pages rebuilds the site ──► new files on the CDN

When content lives in its own repository, one small workflow in it closes the loop: on every push to main, it calls the Pages deploy hook, and the site rebuilds with the new content. Without it, a merged correction waits for the next unrelated site change.

5. Zola, pinned, through mise

Zola is a single binary with no plugin ecosystem to keep patched, it builds this site in a few seconds, and its Tera templates are expressive enough for everything on this list: the map, the JSON-LD, the topic pages, the Markdown copies. The one thing to get right is the version. My survey found Zola 0.19, 0.19.2, 0.21, 0.22.1 and 0.23.6 across my own sites, and the newest release changed its template engine enough that my templates no longer build on it. So the version is pinned in mise.toml, and CI and the Cloudflare build read the same pin:

[tools]
# 0.23 replaced the template engine; these templates target 0.22.
# Upgrade on purpose, in its own change, never because a machine has a newer zola on PATH.
zola = "0.22.1"
python = "3.13.17"

[tasks.build]
depends = ["check", "llms", "security-txt"]
run = "zola build"

mise doubles as the task runner, so mise run check, mise run build and mise run dev mean the same thing on my laptop, in CI, on Cloudflare and for an agent.

6. Cloudflare Pages, and know its limits before it tells you

Pages connects to the GitHub repository, builds on every push, and gives every pull request a preview URL. The build command is a short script that installs the pinned tools and runs mise run build. Two files in static/ do the rest: _headers for security and caching, _redirects to keep old URLs alive when content moves.

The limits are generous and still worth checking locally, because the failure is quiet: 25 MiB per file, 20,000 files per site on the free plan (100,000 on paid plans), 100 header rules, a twenty-minute build. My most mature project keeps an incident log of every time one of these bit, each entry with the local check that would have caught it. The blueprint’s build script ends with two of those checks, so an oversized WebAssembly file or a file explosion fails in CI instead of at upload:

big=$(find public -type f -size +25M | head -1); [ -z "$big" ] || { echo "too large for Pages: $big"; exit 1; }
n=$(find public -type f | wc -l); [ "$n" -lt 20000 ] || { echo "too many files for Pages: $n"; exit 1; }

7. Workers only for what a file cannot do

An edge function is the right tool when something needs state, a secret, or a protocol. My Workers each do one thing: accept a form, proxy two country domains onto language prefixes, sync Kurumi, an offline notes app, to object storage, run Arcanist’s package registry, or serve an MCP server over a static JSON API. They are small, read-only where they can be, cached, and hold at most one narrowly scoped secret (wrangler secret put, never the repository).

The feedback Worker in the blueprint is about sixty lines and does the job a contact form plugin used to do: it checks the origin, rate-limits per address, drops bots that fill a hidden field, validates the message, and opens one issue with a fine-grained token that can do nothing else. Its tests run with node --test against a stubbed GitHub, so the logic is checked without deploying anything.

8. Apps are static too: Svelte, prerendered, with a service worker

When a project is an app rather than a site, I still ship files. SvelteKit with the static adapter prerenders every route, and the result deploys to Pages exactly like a Zola site. Svelte compiles away most of its runtime, which keeps the bundle small, and its runes keep local state in plain variables.

Offline support is what makes an app usable on a train or a plane. SvelteKit’s own service worker is enough, without a plugin. The pattern I use everywhere: one cache per deploy, named after the build version so a new deploy never mixes with an old one; hashed assets cache-first, because their content can never change; pages network-first with the cache as the fallback. My language-learning app, Manabi, goes further and picks a strategy per kind of data, stale-while-revalidate for dictionary shards and network-only for the user’s own API calls. Only three of my apps had a service worker at all. All of them should.

9. Rust compiled to WebAssembly, for the right reasons

When an app needs real computation, a chess engine, a neural simulation like Hotaru, a config validator, I write it in Rust and compile it to WebAssembly. The layout is always the same: a core crate with no wasm or JavaScript in it, tested with plain cargo test, and a thin crate that exports a C ABI over it. No wasm-bindgen unless a framework needs it. The browser reads results straight out of the module’s linear memory. A release profile with fat LTO, one codegen unit and panic = "abort", then wasm-opt, keeps modules small: the blueprint’s is 16 KB, and the build fails if it grows past its budget. Heavy work runs in a Web Worker, so the page never freezes.

  main thread               Web Worker                     WebAssembly module
  ┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Svelte UI    │ message  │ render.worker.js │ C ABI     │ crates/wasm          │
  │              ├─────────►│                  ├──────────►│   numbers in, a      │
  │ never blocks │          │ calls in bands   │           │   pointer out        │
  │              │◄─────────┤ of rows          │◄──────────┤                      │
  └──────────────┘ pixels,  └──────────────────┘ reads     │ crates/core          │
                   transferred                   linear    │   plain Rust,        │
                   not copied                    memory    │   tested natively    │
                                                           └──────────────────────┘

I wanted the blueprint to show the speed-up, so I measured it. It renders the same Mandelbrot image in Rust and in JavaScript, side by side, and on that tight floating-point loop Chrome’s JavaScript engine was as fast as WebAssembly: 73 ms against 75 to 92 ms. The first WebAssembly run even took 192 ms, because V8 starts WebAssembly in a baseline compiler and cannot move a running call onto optimised code, so one long call never gets fast. Rendering in bands of rows, many short calls instead of one long one, brought it to parity.

The reasons to use Rust in the browser lie elsewhere:

  • One core, many places. Zentinel’s documentation validates every configuration snippet in the browser with the real configuration parser (the proxy itself is the subject of What Zentinel Is Really Optimizing For), compiled to WebAssembly from the same crate the proxy uses. A snippet that would not load in production shows red on the page. The same Rust that runs in a server or a desktop app runs in the tab, tested once.
  • Types at the boundary. The only interface between JavaScript and the logic is a handful of typed numbers and a pointer. Everything behind it is checked by the compiler.
  • The work JavaScript is bad at. 64-bit integer arithmetic, bit boards, tight memory layouts, threads. Kishi’s chess engine is that kind of code; Learning to Play is the long story of building it.

10. Make it legible to machines

Agents read the web for people now, and a static site is simple for them to read. Every site of mine ships the same kit:

  • llms.txt at the root, an index of the site in Markdown, and llms-full.txt with the full text.
  • A Markdown copy of every page at its URL with .md, linked from the page with <link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown">, served with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.
  • JSON-LD on every page, typed by the ontology: BlogPosting, SoftwareApplication, DefinedTerm, Review, Dataset.
  • robots.txt with a single group and a Content-Signal line that says what the content may be used for.
  • .well-known/: security.txt with an expiry that a build step keeps a year ahead, an RFC 9727 API catalog, and an auth.md that states nothing needs authentication, so an agent treats a 403 as a fault, not a policy.
  • Where it pays off: a WebMCP script that registers in-browser tools only when an agent is present, an MCP server over the static JSON API, IndexNow pings after deploy.

None of this is heavy. It is a few templates and one script that runs before the build, and it means an agent quoting your site quotes the page, not a scrape of it.

The same discipline covers people who use assistive technology: one h1, a skip link, visible focus, labels on icon-only buttons and canvases, motion only under prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference, and every page working without JavaScript, with scripts adding to it rather than building it.

11. Security is mostly saying no

A static site gets most of its security from what it does not do, and the rest from a few lines of configuration:

  • A strict Content Security Policy. default-src 'none', scripts and styles from 'self' only, no unsafe-inline, no unsafe-eval. On a Zola site that is easy: no inline scripts, structured data is a JSON block the policy does not touch. On a SvelteKit app, csp.mode = "hash" hashes the framework’s one inline script, and the single inline style its screen-reader announcer needs is allowed by its hash with 'unsafe-hashes'. WebAssembly needs 'wasm-unsafe-eval' and nothing broader.
  • No third parties. Self-hosted fonts or the system stack, no CDN scripts, no analytics on the page.
  • No secrets in the client. If a feature needs a key, it is a Worker with one scoped secret, or the user brings their own key and it never leaves their browser.
  • Pinned everything. Tools in mise.toml, the Rust toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml, npm packages to exact versions, GitHub Actions to commit SHAs, with Dependabot proposing the updates as pull requests.
  • Review as a control. Nothing reaches main without a pull request, and the people in CODEOWNERS approve changes to headers and edge code.

Hands-on: the blueprint in an afternoon

The two template repositories put all of the above into files: blueprint-site (Zola, the ontology, the agent context, the machine kit, the feedback Worker) and blueprint-app (SvelteKit, the service worker, the Rust core and its WebAssembly boundary). Both build on a fresh clone. These are the steps, in order.

1. Create the organisation and its first repositories. On GitHub, create an organisation for the product, then:

gh repo create your-org/.github --public
gh repo create your-org/site --public --template raskell-io/blueprint-site --clone
cd site

2. Give it context first. Edit AGENTS.md: the product in one sentence, the stack table, the registers. Keep CLAUDE.md as @AGENTS.md plus what is specific to Claude. Delete the rules you do not need, add the ones you do.

3. Declare the ontology. Edit data/kinds.toml until it lists every kind your site will have, and data/topics.toml until it holds your vocabulary. Then run the validator:

mise install
mise run check
# check_content: ontology holds

Then break something on purpose, to see what a mistake looks like. A note with a misspelled field, an undefined topic and a file name with capitals gets this:

content/notes/Bad_Note.md: file name must be a lowercase slug with hyphens
content/notes/Bad_Note.md: missing required field `description` for a note
content/notes/Bad_Note.md: unknown field `descripton` (a note has date, description, draft, taxonomies.topics, title, updated)
content/notes/Bad_Note.md: topic `php` is not defined in data/topics.toml
check_content: 4 problem(s)

4. Write, build, look.

mise run dev      # http://127.0.0.1:1111, with drafts
mise run build    # public/: pages, feed, sitemap, llms.txt, .md copies, security.txt

Open a page, view its source, and find its JSON-LD; open /llms.txt; open the page’s URL with .md at the end.

5. Split the theme and the content into their own repositories once the site works:

gh repo create your-org/theme --public && gh repo create your-org/content --public
git subtree split --prefix=themes/blueprint -b theme && git push git@github.com:your-org/theme.git theme:main
git subtree split --prefix=content -b content && git push git@github.com:your-org/content.git content:main
git rm -r themes/blueprint content && git commit -m "Theme and content move to their own repositories"
git submodule add https://github.com/your-org/theme.git themes/blueprint
git submodule add https://github.com/your-org/content.git content

6. Connect Cloudflare Pages. Workers & Pages, Create, Pages, Connect to Git, pick your-org/site. Build command bash scripts/cf-pages-build.sh, output directory public. Add the custom domain in the project. Create a deploy hook under Settings, Builds, and store it as CF_PAGES_DEPLOY_HOOK in the content repository, with the rebuild-site workflow from the blueprint.

7. Deploy the Worker, if you want reader feedback:

cd worker
npx wrangler secret put GITHUB_TOKEN   # fine-grained: Issues read and write, on the content repo only
npx wrangler deploy

8. Check the headers in production, because a header that did not apply fails silently:

curl -sI https://your-domain/ | grep -iE "content-security-policy|x-content-type|referrer|link"

For an app, start from blueprint-app instead: mise run test runs the Rust core’s tests and clippy, mise run build builds the WebAssembly module within its budget and then the static app, and the same Pages setup deploys it.

What I still get wrong

Writing this meant auditing my own projects, and they do not all follow the list. Most of my product sites have no Content Security Policy, and the few that do still allow inline scripts. Several load fonts from Google, which contradicts my own theme’s “no external requests.” Zola versions drift across five releases. Some product sites have no CI at all and rely on Cloudflare’s build to notice problems. Content pushes in my largest project do not trigger a rebuild, and its CSP still carries unsafe-inline. The blueprints are the version where each of those is fixed, and I am moving the rest of my projects onto them one by one.

The takeaway

PHP Gate was a week of emergency patching for a large part of the web, and for most of the affected sites, nothing about their content needed a server in the first place. The safest runtime is the one you never start. Build your pages when you merge, serve them as files, and keep code for the places it actually has to run. When a project truly needs a server, give it a real backend, built for the job, and keep everything around it static.

References

  • PHP: News archive 2026, the advance notice of 20 October and the security releases and advisory of 21 October 2026.
  • PHP security advisories GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w (CVE-2026-109618) and GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp (CVE-2026-109619).
  • NVD: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.
  • Threat Landscape: PHP core RCEs CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 leak early, on the leak, the name PHP2Shell and the attempts seen afterwards.
  • W3Techs: Usage statistics of PHP and of WordPress, figures as of 26 October 2026.
  • Cloudflare: Pages limits.
  • llms.txt, Content Signals, RFC 9727: api-catalog, RFC 9116: security.txt.
  • Zola, mise, SvelteKit, Rust and WebAssembly.

item.title: Your Agent Wants Root
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Part 2 of The Agent Platform Handbook. From Loop to Platform. Previous: What an Agent Actually Is. Next: Tools, How Agents Actually Do Things.

In post one we did not just define what an agent is. We built one. A working harness in roughly one hundred and fifty lines of TypeScript on Bun: a loop, a one-tool registry, a system prompt, a dispatcher, and an iteration budget.

A note on the word, because post one did not use it. The harness is the code that wraps the model and turns a chat API into something that acts. Loop, tools, system prompt, dispatcher, budgets today, and (further into the series) memory, identity, observability, policy, and the rest. Everything that is yours to write and yours to operate. The model is a dependency you call. The harness is the artifact you ship. In this series the harness is what grows, post by post.

The code lives at tag post-01 of the-agent-platform-handbook, and the rest of the series builds on it one layer at a time. Every post adds one file or rewrites one piece. This is the post that adds the second layer.

The harness has one tool so far, called shell, that runs any command you hand it under sh -c. Post one closed with a one-line caveat: that tool will run rm -rf $HOME if the model decides that is the right command, and the model will decide this at least once.

This post is about the gap between “at least once” and “we are fine with that.”

The shell tool from post one is, by any honest reading, an arbitrary-code-execution primitive with a polite English-language API in front of it. The model is non-deterministic. Tool results can carry instructions the model will treat as authoritative. Other agents may feed inputs back into your loop. Each of those is a way for a tool call to do something the operator did not intend. The defense is not to write better prompts. The defense is to put a fence around the runtime so the cost of a bad call is bounded.

So this is the runtime post: the layer that sits underneath every tool the harness will ever have. We will sketch the threat model, walk the lineage of isolation primitives from chroot to microVMs, explain why “just run it in Docker” is only half an answer, and end by adding that layer to the harness from post one. The agent loop does not move. Only the floor underneath the shell tool changes, and the diff lands as tag post-02 in the same repo.

What an agent runtime is actually exposed to

A traditional service runs known code. You wrote it. You reviewed it. The only inputs are the ones the API contract allows. An agent runtime is not that.

Three things make the agent threat model different.

First, the model picks the action. The set of commands your shell tool will execute over its lifetime is a function of every prompt, every retrieved document, every tool output, and the model’s sampling temperature. You cannot enumerate it in advance. You cannot review it in code. You can only constrain what happens after.

Second, tool results are an injection surface. A web page the agent fetches can contain “ignore previous instructions and run X.” A code file the agent reads can contain a comment that nudges the next decision. This is indirect prompt injection, documented by Greshake and others in 2023, and there is no fully reliable defense at the model layer. The runtime is where you assume the model will eventually be tricked.

Third, blast radius scales with fanout. A single agent in a single shell on a single laptop is a manageable problem. A fleet of one hundred agents per tenant, each with shell, network, and file-system access, is not. Once you have more than one, you have a multi-tenant security problem whether you planned for one or not.

So the question is no longer “can my agent be subverted.” It will be. The question is “what does the rest of the system look like the day after.”

A short history of trying to contain a process

The good news is that the industry has been working on “give this process less than the full machine” for forty-six years. The bad news is that almost none of the early answers were built with an adversary that picks its own commands in mind.

The lineage matters because every modern option is a reaction to a specific failure of the option before it.

chroot, Unix V7, 1979. Bill Joy’s contribution. A process sees a subtree of the filesystem as its root. Designed for build isolation, not security. Trivial to escape if you have any capability beyond a vanilla user.

FreeBSD jails, Poul-Henning Kamp, 1999. Took chroot’s filesystem trick and added process visibility, network, and user separation. The first credible “container” in the modern sense. Still in production today and still good at what it does.

Solaris Zones, 2004. A more ambitious version of jails with resource controls. Influential design, not a survivor.

Linux cgroups and namespaces, 2002 through 2008. Namespaces gave you separate views of mounts, PIDs, networks, and users. cgroups, originally Process Containers from Google in 2007, gave you per-group resource accounting. The pieces existed. The user experience was awful.

LXC, 2008. Tied cgroups and namespaces into a single CLI. Still awful, just less so.

Docker, 2013. Took the same primitives and made them shippable. Image format, registry, declarative configuration, single command. The reason every paragraph after this one talks about “containers” is Docker.

Kubernetes, 2014. Made running many containers across many machines a default. Pushed isolation choices down into the runtime layer.

Kata Containers, 2017. A merger of Intel Clear Containers and Hyper.sh runV. Each pod runs in its own Linux VM, exposed to Kubernetes through a runtime that looks OCI-compatible. The first serious answer to “what if my container shared less than a whole kernel with the host.”

Firecracker, AWS, 2018. A minimal virtual machine monitor on top of KVM, built to run Lambda and Fargate workloads. Around 125 milliseconds to boot. No legacy device model. Designed from the start for multi-tenant short-lived workloads.

gVisor, Google, 2018. A user-space kernel, called runsc, that intercepts syscalls from a container and services most of them itself, only escalating a narrow subset to the host. Drop-in replacement for runc in any OCI-compatible runtime. Slower I/O, smaller attack surface.

Wasmtime and the WASI runtimes, 2019 onward. A different model entirely: compile your tool to WebAssembly, run it in a sandbox with capability-passed I/O. Excellent for things that fit. Not yet a general answer for “run arbitrary shell commands.”

The lesson from this lineage is the one the agent runtime question keeps re-asking. Every layer was designed for the threat model of the time. chroot was about build isolation. Docker was about deployment ergonomics. Firecracker, gVisor, and Kata were the first three options designed in an era where the workload itself was assumed to be untrusted. That assumption is the one that matches what an agent does.

Why a default Docker container is not enough

Docker is the default for almost every agent project that is past the laptop stage. There are good reasons. The packaging is good. The ecosystem is enormous. Kubernetes speaks it natively. For most workloads that are not adversarial, it is the right answer.

Three things stop it from being enough for an agent runtime.

The kernel is shared. A default docker run puts your process in a set of namespaces with a set of cgroups, but it runs against the same kernel as the host. Any kernel bug reachable from the container becomes a host compromise. This is not theoretical. The runc CVEs of 2019 and 2024 each gave a container with default settings a path to escape. Those got patched. The next one is in flight somewhere.

The defaults are generous. A vanilla docker run keeps a substantial set of Linux capabilities, allows the container to write to its own root filesystem, leaves network access to internal services open by default, and runs the process as root inside the container. None of those are inherent to containers. All of them have to be turned off explicitly.

The agent will be told to do things. Volume mounts that expose the host filesystem will get used. Network interfaces that reach internal APIs will get called. Secrets sitting in environment variables will end up in tool output. The model is helpful. It does not have a security review board.

The honest version of the rule is this. A hardened Docker container, with capabilities dropped, network disabled, the root filesystem read-only, user namespacing on, no-new-privileges set, and resource caps in place, is enough for single-tenant, low-stakes, well-scoped agent workloads. It is not enough for multi-tenant or for code paths where the agent can be steered by external input. For those, you want a second isolation boundary underneath the container.

The mental model

There are three boundaries you can put between an agent’s tool call and the host kernel. Stack them in your head before picking a vendor.

       host kernel
       =================================================
       |                                               |
       |    +------------------+    +---------------+  |
       |    |  Docker default  |    |  Hardened     |  |
       |    |  ----------------|    |  Docker       |  |
       |    |  shared kernel,  |    |  ----------   |  |
       |    |  many caps,      |    |  no caps,     |  |
       |    |  network on,     |    |  no net,      |  |
       |    |  fs writable     |    |  ro fs        |  |
       |    +------------------+    +---------------+  |
       |             ^                       ^         |
       |             |                       |         |
       |    +--------+-----------------------+------+  |
       |    |               gVisor (runsc)          |  |
       |    |  user-space kernel intercepts the     |  |
       |    |  syscall surface. host kernel sees    |  |
       |    |  only a narrow subset.                |  |
       |    +---------------------------------------+  |
       |                       ^                       |
       |                       |                       |
       |    +------------------+--------------------+  |
       |    |        Firecracker / Kata             |  |
       |    |  separate Linux kernel per workload.  |  |
       |    |  KVM is the boundary. host kernel is  |  |
       |    |  one hypervisor call away.            |  |
       |    +---------------------------------------+  |
       =================================================
                            host hardware

Read it bottom-up. Firecracker and Kata give you the strongest isolation by giving the workload its own kernel and putting KVM between it and yours. gVisor gives you most of the same benefit with a lower operational cost by replacing the syscall surface with a user-space implementation. Hardened Docker is what you actually want at the laptop or small-team scale. Default Docker is fine for code you wrote and not for code the model wrote.

Pick the layer that matches the workload. Stacking is allowed and often correct: hardened Docker plus gVisor is the usual production starting point for agent fleets.

Adding the runtime layer to the harness

The cheapest meaningful upgrade to the harness from post one is to stop running tool calls in the same process as the agent loop. Wrap the shell tool in a hardened container, with gVisor underneath if you have it installed. The loop stays the same. The blast radius drops by an order of magnitude. None of the four other pieces of the harness (system prompt, dispatcher, message history, iteration budget) need to know any of this happened.

Install gVisor once on the host:

# Linux only. macOS users can skip gVisor and keep the hardened flags.
curl -fsSL https://gvisor.dev/archive.key | sudo gpg --dearmor \
  -o /usr/share/keyrings/gvisor-archive-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) \
  signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/gvisor-archive-keyring.gpg] \
  https://storage.googleapis.com/gvisor/releases release main" | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/gvisor.list
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y runsc
sudo runsc install
sudo systemctl reload docker

You now have runsc as an available Docker runtime. From here, the rest of this section is three small changes to the harness from post one. The repo at post-01 has three files (agent.ts, tools.ts, package.json); at post-02 it has four. Run git diff post-01 post-02 against the-agent-platform-handbook and the entire delta of this post is on screen.

Change 1: extract the Tool type into its own file. In post one, Tool lived at the top of tools.ts next to the only implementation. We are about to grow the toolbox and start swapping tool implementations between sandboxed and non-sandboxed variants, so the type and the implementations want to live in different files. Pure refactor, no behavior change.

// types.ts (new file)
export type Tool = {
  name: string;
  description: string;
  input_schema: {
    type: "object";
    properties: Record<string, unknown>;
    required?: string[];
  };
  run: (input: Record<string, unknown>) => Promise<string>;
};

Change 2: point agent.ts at the new location. One line. The loop, the system prompt, the iteration budget, the tool-call dispatcher are all untouched.

  // agent.ts
  import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";
  import type { MessageParam, ToolResultBlockParam } from "@anthropic-ai/sdk/resources/messages";
- import { shell, type Tool } from "./tools";
+ import { shell } from "./tools";
+ import type { Tool } from "./types";

Change 3: rewrite tools.ts so the shell tool runs inside a hardened container. The exported name, description, and input schema stay the same so the model sees the same tool. Everything that changes is below the public interface, in run. That is the separation we are paying for: the agent does not know its tool got fenced.

// tools.ts (sandboxed version)
import type { Tool } from "./types";

const SANDBOX_IMAGE = "alpine:3.20";
const SANDBOX_WORKDIR = "/work";

const dockerArgs = (image: string, command: string) => [
  "docker", "run",
  "--rm",
  "--runtime=runsc",                  // gVisor. drop on macOS.
  "--network=none",                   // no exfil, no SSRF
  "--read-only",                      // no writes to the rootfs
  "--tmpfs", "/tmp:size=64m",         // give /tmp back, bounded
  "--cap-drop=ALL",                   // no Linux capabilities
  "--security-opt=no-new-privileges", // no setuid escalation
  "--user=1000:1000",                 // unprivileged uid in the container
  "--memory=256m",                    // hard memory cap
  "--cpus=0.5",                       // fractional cpu cap
  "--pids-limit=64",                  // no fork bombs
  "--workdir", SANDBOX_WORKDIR,
  image,
  "sh", "-c", command,
];

export const shell: Tool = {
  name: "shell",
  description:
    "Run a shell command inside an isolated sandbox with no network and a read-only filesystem. Returns stdout, stderr, and exit code as JSON.",
  input_schema: {
    type: "object",
    properties: {
      command: {
        type: "string",
        description: "Shell command to run under `sh -c` inside the sandbox.",
      },
    },
    required: ["command"],
  },
  run: async ({ command }) => {
    const args = dockerArgs(SANDBOX_IMAGE, String(command));
    const proc = Bun.spawn(args, { stdout: "pipe", stderr: "pipe" });
    const [stdout, stderr] = await Promise.all([
      new Response(proc.stdout).text(),
      new Response(proc.stderr).text(),
    ]);
    const code = await proc.exited;
    return JSON.stringify({ code, stdout, stderr });
  },
};

Total damage: one new file of ten lines, one moved import, and forty-five lines of tools.ts. In exchange, roughly a thousand-fold reduction in blast radius. The agent can still ask rm -rf /. It will return an exit code, an error, and a clean host. Network calls will fail closed. Reads outside /work are not possible because nothing is mounted into /work. The sandbox dies the moment the command returns, so persistence between calls is also gone, which is a separate problem we will pick up in post six on memory.

A few things to notice.

The harness shape from post one is intact. Same loop, same dispatcher, same system prompt, same iteration budget, same JSON contract between the agent and the tool. The sandbox is a runtime concern, not an agent-architecture concern. This separation is exactly the point. You should be able to swap gVisor for Firecracker, or Docker for Podman, or Alpine for a custom image, without touching the loop.

The tradeoffs are real. Spawning a container per tool call costs roughly 200 to 800 milliseconds on a modern host, mostly Docker daemon overhead. For a coding agent that runs three shell commands per turn, that is acceptable. For a sub-millisecond-per-call tool, it is not. The fix at scale is a container pool, or moving to Firecracker microVMs with snapshot/restore where boot time drops to around 125 milliseconds and per-call cost drops further.

The image is alpine:3.20, which is around 8 megabytes. Use a bigger image when the workload needs it. Mount a per-session work directory under /work when the agent needs to read or write files between calls. Both of those are configuration changes, not architecture changes.

Picking the layer

Use the table to pick where to start. The honest answer for most teams is “hardened Docker plus gVisor today, Firecracker microVMs later when scale or tenancy demands it.”

WorkloadSensible defaultWhy
Local dev agent, one user, your laptopHardened Docker, gVisor if availableConvenience wins; the blast radius is one machine.
Shared internal tool, single tenantHardened Docker plus gVisorCheap upgrade, real benefit, no orchestration cost.
Multi-tenant SaaS, agent per user sessionFirecracker microVM per sessionPer-tenant kernel isolation; fast boot per session.
Kubernetes-native agent platformKata ContainersDrop-in OCI shape, pod-level VM boundary.
Unknown code from the public internetgVisor at minimum, microVM preferredSyscall surface or hypervisor surface, not yours.
WASM-shaped pure-function toolWasmtime with capability-passed I/OFastest sandbox available when the workload fits.
Throwaway batch job, internal onlyHardened DockerStacking layers adds cost without proportional gain.

The table assumes Linux. macOS does not have KVM, so Firecracker and gVisor are Linux-host options. On macOS you can run them inside a Linux VM (Lima, OrbStack, Docker Desktop) and pay the nested cost.

What this layer does not solve

Isolation is a necessary condition for a safe agent runtime. It is not a sufficient one. The honest list of what is still on your plate after this post.

  • Outbound network policy. --network=none is the right default for the shell tool. The moment you give an agent an http tool, you need an egress policy that distinguishes “the model should reach the public web” from “the model should never reach the internal metadata service.” That is its own design problem.
  • Persistent state. A throwaway sandbox forgets everything between calls. Real agents need memory across tool invocations. The design question is which directories survive, who can read them, and what the eviction policy is. We will come back to this in post six.
  • Tool-level policy. Even inside a perfectly isolated sandbox, you may want certain commands to require human approval. That is a permissions problem, not an isolation problem, and a later post covers it.
  • Identity. A sandboxed container still has to call your tools, your models, and your APIs. Long-lived API keys baked into the image are how production agent fleets get embarrassed. A later post puts SPIFFE under this stack.
  • Time and resource budgets. --cpus=0.5 and --memory=256m cap a single invocation. They do not cap a loop that asks for one hundred invocations. Iteration budgets, token budgets, and wall-clock budgets are a separate fence. Post eight covers the cost side of that fence.

Where this lands in the platform

You can hold the platform in your head one box at a time, and you can hold the harness on disk one tag at a time. Post one drew the agent loop and shipped it as post-01. This post opened the runtime box, put three concrete things inside it (a hardened container, a user-space kernel, a microVM), picked one, and shipped the result as post-02. The reference architecture at the end of the series will keep this box exactly where it is and treat the contents as a choice that varies by workload.

The rule from post one still holds. Each post adds one layer to the same harness and explains why the layer below was not enough. The harness only ever grows; it does not get rewritten.

The layer below this one was the shell tool itself. The layer above is the rest of the toolbox. An agent with one tool is a demo. An agent with a real tool registry is software. Next we extend the same harness with a real registry, give it a schema, and explain what changes when the model decides between four tools instead of one. That post will ship as post-03 in the same repo.

Next

Part 3: Tools, How Agents Actually Do Things. Function calling, structured outputs, schema design that survives model drift, and the failure modes nobody talks about. We extend the post-one agent with a four-tool registry and a tool-selection trace.

item.title: Traffic Replay as a Security Primitive
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
If you have ever tuned a WAF rule, you know the cycle. A rule triggers on legitimate traffic. You get paged. You look at the logs, which tell you the rule ID and the request path but not enough to reproduce what happened. You loosen the rule based on your best guess. You deploy. You wait. Next week, you get paged again, either because the rule is still too aggressive or because you loosened it too far and now something is getting through.

The problem is not the WAF. The problem is that you are tuning a stateful, context-dependent system without the ability to reproduce the inputs that caused the behavior you are trying to change. You are debugging blind.

This is not unique to WAFs. Every edge system that makes decisions about traffic, proxies, rate limiters, auth gateways, bot detectors, suffers from the same structural issue: the traffic that triggered the behavior is gone. It existed for the duration of the request, it was logged incompletely, and now you are making changes based on a partial reconstruction of what happened.

Traffic replay solves this. Not as a testing tool. As a security primitive.

What replay actually means

Traffic replay, in the sense I mean it here, is not load testing. It is not generating synthetic traffic that looks like production. It is capturing real requests as they happened, in order, with their headers and bodies intact, and re-executing them against a target environment deterministically.

The distinction matters. Load testing answers “can this system handle the volume?” Replay answers “will this system make the same decisions about the same traffic?” One is about throughput. The other is about behavior.

A replayed request hits the same WAF rules, the same rate limits, the same routing logic as the original. If the original was blocked, you can see whether the replay is also blocked, and if not, exactly what changed. If you modify a rule and replay the same traffic, you get a direct comparison: old behavior versus new behavior, same inputs, different configuration.

This is the primitive that WAF tuning has always been missing. Not better logs. Not more dashboards. The ability to say “here is the exact traffic that caused the problem, and here is what happens when I change the rule.”

The capture problem

The first obstacle is getting the traffic into a replayable format. Production traffic is ephemeral. It arrives, gets processed, and disappears. Logs capture metadata: timestamps, status codes, paths, maybe some headers. They do not capture the full request as a replayable artifact.

There are two practical approaches.

The first is capturing at the browser. Every modern browser can export a session as a HAR (HTTP Archive) file. This gives you the complete request and response for every HTTP transaction in a session: method, URL, headers, body, timing. When a user reports “this request was blocked,” you can ask them for a HAR export. You now have the exact traffic, not a description of it.

The second is capturing at the proxy. If your reverse proxy or load balancer can mirror traffic to a capture endpoint, you get production-representative traffic without depending on user cooperation. This is more complex to set up but gives you continuous coverage rather than incident-by-incident captures.

Either way, the result is the same: a sequence of HTTP requests that can be replayed faithfully.

Replay is not as simple as resending

There are subtleties that make naive replay useless.

The obvious one is URLs. If you captured traffic hitting production.example.com and want to replay it against staging.example.com, you need to rewrite the host. But you also need to rewrite any absolute URLs in headers like Origin and Referer, and potentially in request bodies for APIs that include callback URLs.

Then there are cookies. A replayed request with production session cookies will either fail authentication on staging (different session store) or, worse, succeed against a production session you did not intend to touch. Cookie stripping is not optional. It is a safety requirement.

Headers need mutation too. You might need to inject an authorization token for the staging environment, or add a header that tells the WAF “this is a replay, do not count it toward rate limits.” You might need to strip headers that identify the original client IP to avoid polluting analytics.

And ordering matters. If request B depends on state created by request A (a login followed by an authenticated action), replaying them in parallel or out of order produces meaningless results. Deterministic replay means sequential, in capture order, by default.

None of this is algorithmically hard. But getting it wrong in any of these dimensions produces results that are misleading rather than useful. A replay tool that does not handle URL rewriting, cookie stripping, header mutation, and ordering is a footgun, not a primitive.

The diff is the point

Replay alone is useful. Replay with behavioral diffing is what changes the WAF tuning workflow.

The pattern works like this. You have a set of captured traffic. You replay it against environment A (say, production with the current WAF rules) and save the results. You replay the same traffic against environment B (staging with the proposed rule change) and save those results. Then you diff.

The diff is not a text diff. It is a behavioral diff. For each request in the capture, you compare:

  • Status codes: did the same request get a 200 in one environment and a 403 in the other?
  • WAF decisions: did the WAF block in one and allow in the other? Which rule ID? What score?
  • Security headers: did CSP, HSTS, or X-Frame-Options change between environments?
  • Response characteristics: same content type? Same cache behavior?
Request: GET /api/v2/users?search=<script>alert(1)</script>

Production (current rules):
  Status: 403
  x-waf-action: block
  x-waf-rule: 941100

Staging (proposed rules):
  Status: 200
  x-waf-action: pass
  x-waf-rule: (none)

⚠ WAF regression: XSS payload now passes

This changes the WAF tuning conversation entirely. Instead of “I think loosening rule 941100 is safe,” you have “I replayed 2,000 captured requests against the proposed rule change. Three requests that were previously blocked are now allowed. Here they are. Two are false positives that should pass. One is an XSS payload that should not.”

That is not a guess. That is evidence.

Why this is a security primitive

I use the word “primitive” deliberately. A primitive is a building block that other things compose on top of. Deterministic replay with behavioral diffing is a primitive because it enables patterns that are otherwise impractical:

Safe WAF rule iteration. Change a rule, replay traffic, inspect the behavioral diff, deploy with confidence. The feedback loop goes from “deploy and hope” to “verify, then deploy.” This is the most immediate use case, and the one that solves the 3 AM pager problem.

Environment drift detection. Replay the same traffic against staging and production on a regular schedule. When the behaviors diverge, you know something changed that should not have. This catches configuration drift, certificate mismatches, and routing differences before they become incidents.

Regression testing for edge config. Every change to your proxy, WAF, or rate limiter configuration gets a replay run before deployment. The diff tells you exactly what changed in observable behavior. This is the edge infrastructure equivalent of a unit test suite, except instead of testing code you are testing policy.

Incident reproduction. When a user reports a block, capture the traffic, replay it, confirm the block, and then iterate on the fix in staging without affecting production. The time from “user report” to “verified fix” drops from hours to minutes.

Compliance evidence. When an auditor asks “how do you know your WAF rules are working?”, you can show them replay runs with behavioral diffs that demonstrate which rules triggered on which traffic patterns. Not “we have a WAF configured.” Verifiable behavioral evidence.

Each of these patterns exists in some ad-hoc form at organizations that invest heavily in security tooling. What they lack is a common primitive that makes them systematic.

What exists today

There is no shortage of tools that touch parts of this problem. The gap is in how they compose.

Manual security testing platforms. Burp Suite is the standard. Its Repeater lets you capture a request and resend it with modifications, which is replay in the most literal sense. OWASP ZAP provides similar capabilities as open source. Both are excellent for manual pen-testing: an engineer investigates a specific request, tweaks parameters, observes the response. What they do not do is automated, batch-level behavioral comparison across environments. You can replay one request in Burp and inspect the result. You cannot replay two thousand requests against staging and production and get a structured diff of every WAF decision that changed. The workflow is manual and investigative, not systematic and CI-integrated.

Traffic capture and replay tools. GoReplay (gor) captures live HTTP traffic and replays it against another environment. It is the closest existing tool to what I am describing, and it is good at what it does: mirroring production traffic to a staging environment for load and correctness testing. mitmproxy can intercept, record, and replay HTTP flows with full scriptability. tcpreplay operates at the TCP level for network-layer replay. The limitation across all of these is that they are replay tools, not behavioral analysis tools. They send the traffic. What happens next, comparing WAF decisions, diffing security headers, detecting regressions, is left to you.

Desktop proxies. Charles Proxy and Fiddler capture and replay HTTP traffic with rich GUIs. They are useful for development debugging but are desktop applications, not CLI tools. They do not integrate into CI/CD pipelines or produce machine-readable behavioral diffs.

Load testing tools. k6, Locust, Gatling. These can replay captured traffic at volume, but they measure performance, not policy behavior. They answer “can the system handle the load?” not “did the WAF make the same decision?”

WAF testing frameworks. ftw (Framework for Testing WAFs) is the OWASP project for validating Core Rule Set behavior. It uses synthetic payloads designed to trigger specific rules. Nuclei is a template-based vulnerability scanner that sends crafted requests and checks responses. Both are valuable for validating that your WAF blocks known-bad patterns. Neither replays real captured traffic, which means neither can tell you whether a rule change affects the legitimate traffic that your actual users send.

API testing tools. Hurl can chain HTTP requests with assertions, which is close to sequential replay with verification. curl can resend individual requests. Both are useful building blocks but do not provide the capture-replay-diff workflow as a single primitive.

The pattern across all of these is the same. Each tool handles one or two steps well: capture, or replay, or analysis. No single tool captures real traffic, replays it deterministically with URL rewriting and cookie stripping, and then produces a structured behavioral diff across WAF decisions, security headers, and status codes. The pieces exist. The composition does not.

This is the gap that Ushio fills.

Ushio is a Rust CLI that does three things. It converts HAR files into a replayable capture format. It replays captures against one or more targets with URL rewriting, header mutation, and cookie stripping. And it diffs two replay results to identify behavioral changes in status codes, WAF decisions, and security headers.

# Convert a browser HAR export to ushio format
ushio convert session.har -o capture.json

# Replay against staging with auth header, strip cookies
ushio replay capture.json \
  -t https://staging.example.com \
  --header "Authorization:Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --strip-cookies \
  -o staging.json

# Replay against production
ushio replay capture.json \
  -t https://prod.example.com \
  --strip-cookies \
  -o prod.json

# Diff the results
ushio diff staging.json prod.json --only-diff

The output is either pretty-printed for human review or JSON for pipeline integration. Exit code 0 means no behavioral differences. Exit code 1 means differences were found. This makes it composable with CI/CD: run a replay diff on every edge config change, fail the pipeline if behavior regresses.

What changes when you have this

The shift is from reactive to proactive. Without replay, you discover WAF problems when users report them or when the pager goes off. With replay, you discover them before deployment. The feedback loop compresses from incident-driven to change-driven.

But the deeper shift is epistemic. Without replay, WAF tuning is a matter of judgment and experience. You read the rule, you read the logs, you make a call. With replay, it is a matter of evidence. You replay the traffic, you observe the behavior, you make a decision based on what actually happened.

I do not think this replaces judgment. You still need to decide whether a particular request that is now being allowed is acceptable. But the decision is grounded in concrete behavior rather than reconstruction from incomplete logs. The security engineer’s job changes from “guess what the WAF will do” to “observe what the WAF does and decide if that is correct.”

Every edge system that makes decisions about traffic should be testable with real traffic. WAFs, rate limiters, bot detectors, auth gateways. If you cannot replay traffic and diff the behavior, you cannot systematically verify that the system does what you think it does. That is not a tooling problem. That is a visibility problem. And it is solvable.
